steps.text: 2 cups (18oz/510g) self-rising or all-purpose flour (See tips below)
2 tablespoons of butter or vegetable oil
1/2 teaspoon of vanilla extract (optional)
Crack the eggs into a bowl and beat until creamy. Add in the dry ingredients (excluding the salt and baking soda if using self-rising flour). Do not stir the mixture at this point!
Melt the butter in a microwave-safe bowl. Make sure that it's completely melted; about a minute is sufficient.
Add the butter and milk to the mix. Stir gently, leaving some small clumps of dry ingredients in the batter.
Overmixing your batter is going to develop strong gluten strains, which will make your pancakes very chewy.
Heat the frying pan to a medium-low flame.
Sprinkle a few flecks of water onto your pan.
Pour about 3 tablespoons to 1/4 cup batter from the tip of a large spoon or from a pitcher onto the hot griddle or greased frying pan.
Cook for about two minutes or until the pancake is golden.
Cook the other side until golden and remove.
In Python, strings are immutable . Changing a string does not modify the string. It creates a new one.
Strings are sliceable. Slicing a string gives you a new string from one point in the string, backwards or forwards, to another point, by given increments.
Scenario: Developer wants to transform a string
Transformation is to reverse order of all the characters
example01 produces the desired result, using extended slice notation .
Developer might expect something like string.reverse()
The native idiomatic (aka " pythonic ") solution may not be readable to newer developers
Developer may be tempted to implement his or her own version of string.reverse() to avoid slice notation.
The output of slice notation may be counter-intuitive in some cases: see e.g., example02 print 'coup_ate_grouping'[-4:] ## => 'ping'
print 'coup_ate_grouping'[-4:-1] ## => 'pin'
the different outcomes of indexing on [-1] may throw some developers off
